title: A Well for the Choir
premise: Elodie Delacroix returns to her family's decaying Louisiana house to bury her twin brother Elias—only to learn at the funeral that the body in the casket was actually hers, and Elias is the one who came home. As the mirrors in the house begin lagging a second behind reality, Elias realizes their grandmother's choir of the dead has mistaken him for the sibling who was promised to it, and the song it has been humming for generations is missing only its final verse—a verse that requires his voice. Racing his sister's ghost through the house's shifting rooms, Elias must learn the verse from Elodie without ever singing along, because joining the choir means taking his place among the mirrors forever. In the end he sings the verse alone as an offering, not a surrender, trading his own reflection for Elodie's freedom, and leaves the house with one mirror dark and one sibling's song finally finished.
about_author: Orsen Almeida is a former church organist from the Gulf Coast who spent a decade transcribing hymns from defunct congregations before turning to fiction. His work explores what families inherit when the will is silent and the singing will not stop.

chapters.title: The Wrong Casket
chapters.summary: POV Elias. At the funeral, Elias recognizes the dead woman as his twin Elodie, not himself—yet everyone calls the body Elias Delacroix. The emotional beat is vertigo: he is grieving his sister while the world insists he is the corpse. He touches the casket and his reflection in its brass rail arrives a beat too late.

chapters.title: Lights On, Doors Counted
chapters.summary: POV Elias. He moves into the Delacroix house to settle the estate, following Elodie's childhood rituals: every light burning, doors counted at dusk. The house feels expectant rather than empty. The beat is uneasy belonging—he has nowhere else, and the house seems to know it.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: POV Elias. In the hallway mirror, his reflection lags: he lowers his arm and the glass follows a full second later. He tests every mirror in the house; all of them are late. The beat is dread sharpening into curiosity—the delay is growing.

chapters.title: Elodie in the Glass
chapters.summary: POV Elias. The delayed reflection stops being his. Elodie stands in the mirror, mouthing words he cannot hear, pointing down the hall. The beat is desperate joy and terror in equal measure—his sister exists, and she is afraid of something behind him.

chapters.title: The Choir's Hymnal
chapters.summary: POV Elias. In the attic he finds Grand-mère's hymnal, its last page torn out, margins crowded with names—every Delacroix for a century, most marked with a date of death that isn't theirs. The beat is the weight of inheritance: the family has been paying something off for generations.

chapters.title: What Grand-mère Promised
chapters.summary: POV Elias via Elodie's mirror-speech and letters. He pieces together the bargain: the choir of the dead keeps the family safe from the thing beneath the well, and in exchange one twin per generation joins the singing. This generation, it was meant to be Elodie. The beat is horrified understanding.

chapters.title: The Thing Under the Well
chapters.summary: POV Elias. Drawn to the old wellhouse, he hears the choir's true audience: something vast below, listening patiently, humming along. The beat is cosmic dread—the choir isn't a comfort to the dead; it's a leash on the living dark.

chapters.title: Doors That Weren't There
chapters.summary: POV Elias. The house begins rearranging: a door where the pantry was, the nursery where his bedroom should be. Rooms he counts at dusk are wrong by morning. The beat is losing the ground of home—the house is no longer shelter but a throat.

chapters.title: Learning to Read Her Lips
chapters.summary: POV Elias. He spends nights at the mirror teaching himself Elodie's mouthed words, building a vocabulary from childhood games they invented. The beat is tender, aching reconnection—two siblings rebuilding a language across the boundary of a glass.

chapters.title: The First Verse
chapters.summary: POV Elodie, in mirror-fragments. She explains the song's structure: three verses bind the thing below, and the third was never written down because it must be learned, never sung along to. The beat is instruction as intimacy—she is teaching him to survive her.

chapters.title: A Visitor from the Parish
chapters.summary: POV Elias. Father Aubert, who buried the wrong body, arrives with the parish's old records and a warning: he has seen a Delacroix sing at the window at night. The beat is the outside world intruding—witnesses make the haunting undeniable.

chapters.title: The Choir Rehearses
chapters.summary: POV Elias. At midnight, voices rise from the walls—his ancestors, rehearsing in the plaster. He recognizes Grand-mère's alto among them. The beat is terrible homesickness: the dead sound like family, and they are singing for him to come along.

chapters.title: They Know His Name
chapters.summary: POV Elias. The choir begins calling his name between verses, gently, the way family calls you to dinner. Mirrors fog with breath from the wrong side. The beat is the seduction of belonging—the horror is how welcome he feels.

chapters.title: Elodie's Warning
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Through urgent mirror-signs she warns him: the choir doesn't want his voice for the verse, it wants his consent. Singing along, even one note, is agreement. The beat is protective desperation—she died to keep this from happening.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: POV Elias. He hunts the hymnal's missing last page through the shifting house, finding it framed above Grand-mère's mirror—but the notation is wrong, deliberately corrupted by a hand that wanted no one to sing it correctly. The beat is betrayal across generations.

chapters.title: Father Aubert's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Aubert. Decades ago, Grand-mère asked him to help her cheat the bargain by substituting a twin's name in the parish rolls. He refused; she did it anyway. The beat is guilt and complicity—the church has known, and looked away, for a century.

chapters.title: The House Sings Back
chapters.summary: POV Elias. The house itself joins the choir—floorboards groaning melody, pipes whistling harmony. Doors he counts at dusk are open by dawn, all of them facing the wellhouse. The beat is enclosure: the home is becoming an instrument.

chapters.title: Elodie's Last Day
chapters.summary: POV Elodie, in memory. Flashback to the week before her death: she learned what the choir intended, tried to break the bargain alone, and failed. The beat is tragic agency—she wasn't taken; she fought and lost, and Elias never knew.

chapters.title: Mimicry
chapters.summary: POV Elias. Something in the mirrors begins imitating Elodie—perfectly, except it never blinks. He nearly follows it into the glass before noticing. The beat is paranoia corroding his one lifeline; he can no longer trust the voice he loves.

chapters.title: The Test of the Blink
chapters.summary: POV Elias. He devises tests only the real Elodie would pass—childhood secrets, the wrong words to old songs. The real Elodie surfaces, weakened, and tells him the choir is wearing her to reach him. The beat is relief and grief braided together.

chapters.title: Halfway Verse
chapters.summary: POV Elias. Working from the corrupted page and Elodie's corrections, he learns the first half of the true verse. When he hums it silently, the thing under the well goes quiet—for the first time in a century. The beat is fragile hope with a terrible cost: the dark has noticed him.

chapters.title: The Wellhouse Opens
chapters.summary: POV Elias. The wellhouse doors stand open, the well bricked over from below. Cold air carries the smell of the parish cemetery. The beat is the threshold moment—the story's geography turns inside out, and the deep is now the near.

chapters.title: Aubert's Last Rites
chapters.summary: POV Aubert. The old priest attempts an exorcism of the house and is taken mid-liturgy, his voice joining the choir before his body falls. The beat is the failure of institutional salvation—holy words are just words to something that predates them.

chapters.title: What the Choir Wants
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. She reveals the choir's true design: it doesn't guard the family from the dark—it farms them, one voice per generation, feeding the thing just enough song to keep it sleeping. The beat is disillusionment: the inheritance is not protection but livestock.

chapters.title: Elias Stops Sleeping
chapters.summary: POV Elias. He fights exhaustion because the choir comes closest when he dreams, calling in his mother's voice now. The house dims its lights one by one, punishing his wakefulness. The beat is attrition—the horror of being worn down by patience.

chapters.title: The Mirror Room
chapters.summary: POV Elias. He finds a room that is all mirrors, reflecting a choir of Delacroixes stretching back two centuries, every one of them singing with their eyes on him. Grand-mère conducts. The beat is confrontation with the full inheritance—the family tree, arranged as an audience.

chapters.title: Elodie's Sacrifice Offered
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. She offers a way out: if Elias leaves the house and lets the choir take her fully, the verse will never be learned and the cycle continues—but he lives. The beat is the theme made flesh: love against duty, each twin trying to die for the other.

chapters.title: He Refuses
chapters.summary: POV Elias. He refuses to leave, telling her the family's duty ends with their generation—the song stops with them. The choir's response is immediate: every mirror in the house shatters except the one holding Elodie. The beat is defiant love and escalating stakes.

chapters.title: The Dark Rises
chapters.summary: POV Elias. With the bargain fraying, the thing beneath the well stirs fully awake, and the house begins sinking toward it, room by room, like a ship taking on earth. The beat is apocalyptic pressure—the leash has slipped, and the family's century of singing bought nothing permanent.

chapters.title: Learning the Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. In the one surviving mirror, she teaches him the final verse note by note, the way their mother taught them lullabies. He learns it in silence, mouth only, heart pounding against the melody. The beat is the tenderest chapter—love as instruction, grief as curriculum.

chapters.title: The Choir's Bargain Renewed
chapters.summary: POV Elias. The choir offers terms: sing the verse with them and the dark sleeps another century, the house is saved, and Elodie rests. All it costs is his voice, forever, among theirs. The beat is the devil's arithmetic—everything reasonable except the soul.

chapters.title: Counting the Doors One Last Time
chapters.summary: POV Elias. He performs Elodie's ritual one final time—lights on, doors counted—and understands it was never a ward but a countdown, kept by every Delacroix who waited their turn. The beat is quiet devastation: the rituals of home were the rituals of surrender.

chapters.title: The Night of the Verse
chapters.summary: POV Elias. At midnight the house opens every door at once, and the choir sings the first two verses at full strength as the dark rises through the floors. Elias stands at the surviving mirror with the last verse in his mouth and does not open it. The beat is the still point before the climax.

chapters.title: Singing Alone
chapters.summary: POV Elias. He sings the final verse alone—offering it, not joining it—his voice the only one in the house, giving the dark what it was owed as a gift freely ended rather than a debt renewed. The beat is the climax: one mortal voice against a century of harmony, love sung without surrender.

chapters.title: The Silence After
chapters.summary: POV Elias. The dark takes the verse and goes down. The choir, its purpose finished, dissolves note by note—Grand-mère last, nodding once. Elodie's mirror goes dark and ordinary. The beat is exhaustion and release: the song is over, and he is still himself.

chapters.title: Elodie's Farewell
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. In the last hour before the mirror releases her, she and Elias press palms to the glass. She tells him the verse was always meant for a twin to give freely—that was the loophole Grand-mère never found. The beat is grief with peace in it: she goes loved, and free.

chapters.title: Burying the Right Sibling
chapters.summary: POV Elias. He has the casket opened and the records corrected—Elodie's name on the stone, the parish's century of lies amended in ink. He buries her properly, in daylight, with no hymn. The beat is restitution: the dead deserve their true names.

chapters.title: The Dark Mirror
chapters.summary: POV Elias. He packs the house, leaving every mirror intact except Elodie's, which he covers with black cloth and carries to the car. The house, emptied of its song, is just a house—settling, aging, done. The beat is the strange lightness of an ended haunting.

chapters.title: One Second On Time
chapters.summary: POV Elias. Driving away, he stops at a rest-stop mirror and watches his reflection move exactly with him, neither late nor early. He hums nothing. The beat is recovery: time belongs to him again, and silence is a thing he has earned.

chapters.title: A Well for the Choir
chapters.summary: POV Elias, epilogue. Years later he fills in the wellhouse with concrete and plants a garden over it, and on certain evenings he almost hears a third verse being hummed somewhere kind. He does not sing along. He never will. The beat is belonging redefined: he belongs to the living now, and to his sister's memory—kept, counted, and finally at rest.
